captions.instagram:
How does water boil?

Water does not boil because it reaches 100 °C. It boils when its vapour can push back as hard as the air presses down, which is why it boils at 88 °C in Leh and 120 °C in a pressure cooker. Heat a pot, watch the molecules and move the pressure yourself.

→ Water does not just start boiling. First it shimmers, then tiny air bubbles appear, and then the pot begins to sing.
→ At 100 °C bubbles of water vapour survive all the way to the top. That is a rolling boil.
→ Heat is motion. Hotter water means faster molecules, and the fastest ones break free of their neighbours.
→ A bubble can only survive when the water's vapour pressure matches the air pressing down. At sea level, that is 100 °C.
→ Then the temperature stops at 100 °C. Boiling a litre away takes 2,257 kilojoules: seven times the heat that brought it to the boil.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/boilclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does water boil? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Water does not boil because it reaches 100 °C. It boils when its vapour can push back as hard as the air presses down, which is why it boils at 88 °C in Leh and 120 °C in a pressure cooker. Heat a pot, watch the molecules and move the pressure yourself.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/boilclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/boilclear

In this video:
• A pot does not boil all at once. Heat flows from the flame through the steel base into the water, and warm water rises while cool water sinks.
• Temperature is motion. Water molecules never stop moving, and temperature is their average kinetic energy.
• Boiling is a pressure contest. A bubble inside water is squeezed by the air above.
• Then the temperature stops. At the boiling point, extra heat no longer warms the water.
• Change the pressure, move the boiling point. Water boils at about 97 °C in Bengaluru, 92 °C in Shimla, 88 °C in Leh and 70 °C on Everest.
• Salt, lids and safety. A teaspoon of salt in a litre raises the boiling point by only about 0.1 °C, so it does not make water boil faster.
